title: CHAPTER 12: LATER MUGHALS & RISE OF REGIONAL POWERS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The death of Emperor Aurangzeb in 1707 marked the rapid decline of Mughal central authority and paved the way for autonomous regional powers.
Regional polities during this period broadly categorized into Successor States (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Rebel States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats), and Independent Kingdoms (Mysore, Kerala).
In 1717, Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar issued a royal farman granting lucrative duty-free trading rights to the English East India Company in Bengal.
Devastating foreign invasions by Nadir Shah of Persia (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan severely crippled Mughal prestige and military power.
Internal factionalism among Mughal nobility (Turani, Irani, and Hindustani factions) prevented effective administrative governance.

blocks.content: The period after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 AD marks the decline of the Mughal Empire and the simultaneous rise of powerful regional states. This phase is extremely important because it explains how a highly centralized empire disintegrated and how new political forces emerged, ultimately paving the way for British expansion in India. This chapter covers the Later Mughals, reasons for Mughal decline, and the rise of regional powers such as Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, and Rajputs.
After Aurangzeb, a series of weak rulers ascended the Mughal throne. These rulers lacked military ability, administrative efficiency, and strong leadership.

blocks.content: The decline of the Mughal Empire was gradual and resulted from multiple interconnected factors.

cells: Shortage of jagirs and exploitation of peasants

blocks.content: The disintegration of the Mughal Empire created a political vacuum that facilitated the rise of autonomous regional powers and paved the way for British paramountcy.
Repeated foreign invasions shattered the prestige and resources of the Mughal Empire.
Nadir Shah invaded India and plundered Delhi. He carried away enormous wealth including the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor diamond.
Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded India multiple times. The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was fought between Abdali and the Marathas.
With the weakening of Mughal authority, provincial governors and local chiefs asserted independence.

rows: Former Mughal provinces that broke away as imperial control weakened, retaining Mughal administrative structures.

blocks.content: Murshid Quli Khan founded the autonomous state of Bengal. Bengal became economically prosperous due to agriculture and trade.
Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded Awadh. Awadh maintained nominal Mughal loyalty while functioning independently.
Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded the state of Hyderabad. It became one of the most powerful regional states.
The Marathas emerged as the strongest power in India. Shivaji laid the foundation of Maratha power.
The Sikhs organized themselves under Banda Bahadur and later Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
Jats under Suraj Mal and Rajputs asserted regional control.

items: Founders of key successor states frequently asked: Nizam-ul-Mulk (Hyderabad, 1724), Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk (Awadh, 1722), and Murshid Quli Khan (Bengal, 1717).
Farrukhsiyar's Farman of 1717 is often referred to as the 'Magna Carta' of the East India Company in Bengal.
Nadir Shah looted the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) and Koh-i-Noor diamond during the reign of Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' in 1739.
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) crushed Maratha ambitions to succeed the Mughals as the paramount imperial power in India.

blocks.content: Agriculture remained the main occupation. However, excessive taxation and continuous wars caused rural distress.
The decline of central authority led to social insecurity. However, regional cultures flourished.
This period represents the transition from Mughal dominance to British colonial rule. It explains the political vacuum exploited by the British.
Last Mughal emperor – Bahadur Shah Zafar II | Peacock Throne – Nadir Shah | Third Battle of Panipat – 1761 | Autonomous Bengal – Murshid Quli Khan | Hyderabad founder – Nizam-ul-Mulk
